# rebase --exec: run a command after every replayed commit

After this page you can use `git rebase --exec` (or `-x`) to automate running test suites, linters, or build commands after every commit in a series, identify exactly which commit introduces a failure, and resume or modify the rebase sequence when checks fail.

## Thesis

When preparing a branch for code review or merging, running tests on only the tip commit guarantees nothing about the intermediate history. A commit series might build cleanly at the tip while containing broken builds, broken tests, or failing lint checks halfway through. `git rebase --exec <cmd>` automatically inserts execution points into an interactive rebase sequence, stopping immediately if any step returns a non-zero exit code.

This turns manual cherry-picking and per-commit testing into a single automated pipeline across your commit range.

Verified below with **git 2.47.3**.

## Mental model

```text
 standard interactive rebase              interactive rebase with --exec

  pick 8134a61 c1                           pick 8134a61 c1
  pick 0f4c8cf c2                           exec pytest
  pick ec5745f c3                           pick 0f4c8cf c2
                                            exec pytest
                                            pick ec5745f c3
                                            exec pytest
```

When you append `--exec <command>` (or `-x <command>`) to `git rebase`, Git generates an instruction list that places an `exec` instruction after every commit to be replayed. 

1. Git replays a commit onto the target baseline.
2. Git checks out the new commit and executes the shell command in the repository root.
3. If the shell command returns exit status 0, Git proceeds to the next commit.
4. If the shell command returns a non-zero exit status, Git halts the rebase, leaving your working directory at the failing commit so you can fix it.

## Basic syntax and execution

Pass the command as a string argument to `-x` or `--exec`.

```bash
git rebase -x "npm test" main
```

You can pass multiple `-x` flags to execute multiple distinct commands per commit in sequential order:

```bash
git rebase -x "make build" -x "make test" main
```

If a command contains spaces or shell syntax, wrap it in quotes. Git uses your system shell (`/bin/sh` on Unix-like systems) to evaluate the command string.

## Lab: automated commit validation

<!-- file: rebase-exec-demo.sh -->
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Recreate the verified rebase --exec demo (git 2.47.x).
set -euo pipefail
rm -rf /tmp/rebase-exec-demo && mkdir /tmp/rebase-exec-demo && cd /tmp/rebase-exec-demo
git init -b main
git config user.name t
git config user.email t@t

# Base commit
echo "base" > file.txt
git add file.txt
git commit -m "base commit"

# Create feature branch with three commits
git checkout -b feature
echo "c1" >> file.txt
git commit -am "c1"

echo "c2" >> file.txt
git commit -am "c2"

echo "c3" >> file.txt
git commit -am "c3"

# Run rebase --exec across the 3 feature commits against main
git rebase -x 'echo ran-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)' main
```

The command above produced this output:

```text
Rebasing (1/6)
Rebasing (2/6)
Executing: echo ran-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
ran-8134a61
Rebasing (3/6)
Rebasing (4/6)
Executing: echo ran-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
ran-0f4c8cf
Rebasing (5/6)
Rebasing (6/6)
Executing: echo ran-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
ran-ec5745f
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/main.
ec5745f c3
0f4c8cf c2
8134a61 c1
```

Notice how Git prints `Executing: <cmd>` before each execution step and lists the commits processed in sequence.

## Handling test failures

When an `--exec` command fails (returns non-zero exit code), Git stops the rebase immediately before proceeding to the next commit. The commit that failed the test is currently checked out as `HEAD`.

```bash
# Example sequence when a test fails during rebase -x
# 1. Rebase stops at failing commit
# 2. Inspect and fix the issue
$ edit src/lib.rs

# 3. Stage the fixes and amend the current commit
$ git add src/lib.rs
$ git commit --amend --no-edit

# 4. Continue the rebase sequence; execution resumes
$ git rebase --continue
```

If you determine the failure requires deeper rework or want to discard the attempt entirely, you can abort the rebase:

```bash
git rebase --abort
```

## Running exec commands across specific commit ranges

By default, `git rebase -x <cmd> <upstream>` targets all commits between `<upstream>` and your current `HEAD`.

To target only a specific count of recent commits on the current branch without specifying an upstream branch, use relative references:

```bash
git rebase -x "pytest" HEAD~3
```

To run a command across an arbitrary range of commits without changing the base branch:

```bash
git rebase -i -x "go test ./..." HEAD~5
```

When run in interactive mode (`-i`), Git opens your configured editor pre-populated with `exec` lines inserted after every `pick` line. You can manually delete specific `exec` lines if you want to skip testing certain commits (e.g., documentation-only commits).

## Comparison of commit verification strategies

| Strategy | Scope | When It Runs | Pros | Cons |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `git rebase -x <cmd>` | Every commit in range | On demand during rebase | Guarantees bisectability; checks every step in history | Takes longer on large commit ranges |
| `git bisect run <cmd>` | Binary search over range | Debugging historical failures | Fast; finds the culprit in $O(\log N)$ steps | Only tests past commits; doesn't rewrite or fix history |
| Pre-commit hooks | Staged changes only | At `git commit` time | Fast feedback while drafting | Can be bypassed with `--no-verify`; doesn't catch retroactively modified series |
| CI runner | Tip commit of PR | On push to remote | Runs in clean environment | Misses broken intermediate commits within a multi-commit PR |

## Common use cases

### 1. Ensuring git bisect accuracy
If intermediate commits on a branch fail to compile or break tests, running `git bisect` in the future can land on a broken commit that conceals the true bug origin. Running `git rebase -x "make test" origin/main` ensures every single commit in your pull request is independently green and safe for future bisection.

### 2. Auto-formatting or linting every commit
If you need to reformat a series of commits using a code formatting tool:

```bash
git rebase -x "prettier --write . && git commit --amend --no-edit" main
```

*Note: Be careful when chaining `git commit --amend` inside `-x` commands. If the formatter modifies files, amending the commit works cleanly. If no files change, `git commit --amend` will exit zero without error if `--no-edit` is provided.*

### 3. Checking for missing documentation or missing migrations
You can execute custom validation scripts to ensure schema migrations or documentation changes stay in sync with code changes on every commit step:

```bash
git rebase -x "./scripts/validate-schema-migrations.sh" main
```

## Pitfalls

1. **Side-effects in execution commands.** Ensure your `--exec` command does not mutate external databases or remote state outside the local repository. If a rebase fails halfway through, side effects from earlier executed steps will remain active in your environment.
2. **Commands that amend working tree state without committing.** If an exec command modifies tracked files (e.g., an automated linters/formatters) without committing or staging those changes, subsequent `pick` steps during the rebase will halt with dirty working tree errors.
3. **Slow test suites on long commit chains.** Running a 5-minute integration test suite across a 20-commit branch takes over an hour. Prefer fast, focused unit test commands when using `-x`, reserving full integration suites for the branch tip or CI.
4. **Interactive editor interference.** When combining `-x` with explicit interactive flags (`git rebase -i -x ...`), Git opens the editor showing all inserted `exec` lines. Saving and exiting without changes proceeds with all checks. Accidental deletion of lines in the editor removes those execution steps.

## Summary

- Use `git rebase -x <cmd> <upstream>` or `--exec <cmd>` to execute a shell command after every replayed commit.
- If the command returns non-zero, Git pauses the rebase, allowing you to inspect, repair (`git commit --amend`), and resume (`git rebase --continue`).
- Multiple `-x` flags can be chained to run sequential checks per commit.
- `--exec` ensures clean commit history for future `git bisect` sessions by validating every intermediate state.
